chunks: Who and what uses test points. The question: Who/what uses test points?
Many different users rely on test points, both people and machines. Design engineers use them to debug. Factory fixtures use them to check boards.
Programming stations use them to load firmware. Field technicians use them for repairs. Each user needs something different, so you design the points with the user in mind.
Think of a public tap on a water main. A plumber, a city inspector and a meter reader may all use it, but each uses a different fitting.
A test point is the same: one connection, several users. A machine wants a flat, precise spot at a fixed spacing. A technician wants a labeled loop to clip onto.
A programmer wants a standard plug. Satisfying all of them takes a bit of planning.
The same copper pad is used at every stage. Early users are people with instruments; middle users are machines; late users go back to people. The design must work for all.
Bring-up: the first power-on and debugging of a new board. Bed-of-nails fixture: factory spring pins that land on pads.
Programming station: a station that loads firmware and a serial number. Calibration: injecting a known value and storing a correction.
Boundary scan (JTAG): a standard test port that lets a tool check connections between chips. Field technician: a person who repairs products after they have shipped.
Take the 3. 3 volts supply rail of one board. A design engineer clips an oscilloscope probe onto a loop on the top. The factory fixture lands on a flat bottom pad.
A field technician measures it with a meter at a labeled point. A programming station uses a standard debug header (a small plug) to load firmware.
The same net serves four users, each with a different fitting. That is the whole idea.
"Engineers during bring-up and validation use them with scopes and meters.
In production, in-circuit and flying-probe testers, functional test stations, programmers and calibration stations contact them, driven by test software that logs by serial number.
Boundary-scan controllers use the JTAG port. Afterwards, field technicians and failure-analysis engineers use them.
Each user needs something different, like fixture pads, clip loops or a programming header."
